mainTopic: רב's קל וחומר about a שרץ, the language experts a city needs for a סנהדרין, code phrases that point to specific חכמים, and why a city needs 120 men
overview: Just before this, the גמרא said a judge on the סנהדרין must be sharp enough to argue that a שרץ is טהור. רב offers such an argument from a snake, and the גמרא knocks it down by comparing it to a thorn. Next, רב יהודה quotes רב: a city needs two people who can speak the languages and one who can understand them before it can host a סנהדרין. ביתר had three such people and יבנה had four. A ברייתא seems to require more, and the גמרא answers that רב follows a different תנא. Because שמעון התימני 'judged before them,' the גמרא lists code phrases used in sources, such as 'אמרי בי רב' and 'שלחו מתם,' and tells us which חכמים each one means. It corrects two of these along the way. Then it returns to the משנה and explains why a city needs 120 men: judges, rows of students, בטלנין, court staff and witnesses, plus the basic workers every proper city must have. Finally it turns to רבי נחמיה's opinion and begins a ברייתא from רבי that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רב's argument that a creeping creature should be pure
steps.stepSummary: רב builds a קל וחומר: a snake kills and adds טומאה to the world, yet it is טהור, so a שרץ, which does not kill, should surely be טהור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a snake, which kills and so adds impurity to the world, is pure, then a creeping creature that does not kill and does not add impurity should surely be pure!
steps.whatsHappening: רב shows the kind of clever argument a judge should be able to make: a logical case for calling a שרץ טהור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument compares the two creatures. A snake causes more טומאה, because the animals and people it kills become dead bodies that are טמא, yet it is טהור. So a שרץ, which causes less טומאה, should be even more clearly טהור.

keyTerms.meaning: A snake
A small creeping creature. Eight kinds are listed in the תורה as טמא.
Adds impurity to the world
Is it not logical? This is the phrase that signals a קל וחומר.

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody actually holds that a שרץ is טהור. This is a practice argument to show how sharp a judge must be, and the גמרא knocks it down right away.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה נָחָשׁ שֶׁמֵּמִית וּמַרְבֶּה טוּמְאָה, טָהוֹר;
phrases.english: Just as a snake, which kills and so increases impurity, is pure;
phrases.notes: Whatever the snake kills becomes a dead body, which is טמא. That is how it 'adds' טומאה.

phrases.english: a creeping creature, which does not kill and so does not increase impurity,
is it not logical that it should be pure?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This carries out רב's earlier claim that he could make a שרץ טהור through logic.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from the snake, which is טהור even though it adds טומאה

steps.title: Rejecting the argument: think of a thorn
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the קל וחומר. A thorn can also kill, yet it is טהור, so killing has nothing to do with whether something is טמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But that is not right. It is just like an ordinary thorn.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב's argument does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument assumed that a snake's killing should make it more likely to be טמא. A thorn can also injure and kill, and still nobody thinks it is טמא. So killing is not a factor in טומאה, and the snake teaches us nothing about the שרץ.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is not so. This is a phrase of rejection.
It is just like
A thorn

phrases.english: But it is not so;
it is just like an ordinary thorn.
phrases.notes: A thorn can hurt or even kill, yet it is טהור. So the snake's killing proves nothing about טומאה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the קל וחומר from step 1.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Killing has nothing to do with טומאה, as the thorn shows.
steps.whatToRemember: רב's קל וחומר about the שרץ is only a test of sharpness. The thorn shows the logic fails.

steps.title: A city needs language experts to host a court
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: a סנהדרין is not placed in a city unless it has two people who can speak the languages and one who can understand them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: In any city that does not have two people who can speak and one who can listen, a סנהדרין is not placed there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule about the minimum number of language experts a city needs before a סנהדרין can sit there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not every judge has to know every language. The court only needs at least two people who can speak them and one more who can understand them, so it can hear witnesses directly.

keyTerms.meaning: Two people who can speak the languages
One person who can understand them, even if he cannot speak them
They place or seat a court
A סנהדרין, here the smaller court of 23 judges

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
Any city that does not have in it
two to speak and one to listen,
phrases.notes: He means people who can speak, or understand, the seventy languages.

phrases.english: they do not place a Sanhedrin in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new rule from the same speakers, still about what a סנהדרין requires.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A סנהדרין needs at least two people who can speak the languages and one who can understand them.

steps.title: Examples: ביתר had three, יבנה had four
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives history: ביתר had three language experts and יבנה had four, and it names the four from יבנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: In ביתר there were three, and in יבנה there were four: רבי אליעזר, רבי יהושע, רבי עקיבא, and שמעון התימני, who would discuss cases before them while sitting on the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows real courts that met רב's requirement for language experts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows the rule in real life: ביתר had three such people and יבנה had four. The note that שמעון התימני sat on the ground and 'judged before them' sets up the list of code phrases at the end of this section.

keyTerms.meaning: ביתר, a city that had a סנהדרין
יבנה, the seat of the חכמים after the חורבן
Discussed cases in front of them
On the ground

phrases.english: And in Beitar there were three,
and in Yavne four:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Akiva,
and Shimon HaTimni, who would discuss cases before them on the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives real examples of the rule in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: Courts had the language experts רב requires
steps.raayaSupportSource: Historical record of the courts in ביתר and יבנה

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to require three, not two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב with a ברייתא: a court with a third expert is 'wise,' and with a fourth nothing is above it. This suggests more than two experts are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: A third makes it wise, and with a fourth there is nothing above it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a source that seems to clash with רב's number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only calls a court 'wise' once it has a third language expert. That sounds like three is the minimum, while רב said two speakers are enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Wise, meaning a properly qualified court
There is nothing above it, so no more experts are needed

phrases.english: They raised an objection: A third, it is wise;
phrases.notes: 'Third' means a third person in the court who knows the languages.

phrases.english: a fourth, there is none above it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's rule from step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that two speakers are enough
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא sets the 'wise' level at three experts, which suggests two is not enough.

steps.title: רב follows a different תנא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב follows another ברייתא, which says a court with a second expert is wise and with a third nothing is above it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds like this תנא, as it was taught: A second makes it wise, and with a third there is nothing above it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב by showing that a different תנא supports his number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two ברייתות disagree about the numbers. רב is not contradicting the first one by mistake. He simply sides with the second, which counts one fewer expert at each level.

keyTerms.meaning: Like this תנא

phrases.english: He says it in accordance with this tanna,
as it was taught: A second, it is wise;
a third, there is none above it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A dispute between תנאים: רב follows the other ברייתא
steps.terutzMaskana: רב sides with a תנא who sets the numbers one lower, so two speakers are enough.
steps.whatToRemember: רב's 'two speak, one listens' rule matches the ברייתא that says 'a second is wise.'

steps.title: 'Learned before the חכמים' means לוי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts a list of code phrases. 'They learned before the חכמים' refers to לוי, who learned before רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They learned before the חכמים' refers to לוי, from רבי.
steps.whatsHappening: Because step 4 said שמעון התימני 'judged before them,' the גמרא now explains several phrases used in sources and tells us who they refer to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a source says 'learned before the חכמים,' it means a teaching from לוי, the student who studied in front of רבי יהודה הנשיא.

keyTerms.meaning: They learned before the חכמים
לוי, a student of רבי

phrases.english: Learning before the Sages: this is Levi, from Rabbi.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the phrase 'דן לפניהם' from step 4 and opens a list of code phrases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Learned before the חכמים' means לוי, who learned before רבי.

steps.title: 'Judged before the חכמים' means four students
steps.stepSummary: 'They judged before the חכמים' refers to four people: שמעון בן עזאי, שמעון בן זומא, חנן המצרי, and חנניא בן חכינאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They judged before the חכמים' refers to שמעון בן עזאי, שמעון בן זומא, חנן המצרי, and חנניא בן חכינאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the people meant by the phrase 'judged before the חכמים.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: These were great students who discussed הלכה in front of the חכמים but were not ordained judges. This is the same role שמעון התימני had in step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: They discussed or judged before the חכמים
בן עזאי, a famous student
בן זומא, a famous student

phrases.english: Judging before the Sages:

phrases.aramaic: שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן עַזַּאי, וְשִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן זוֹמָא,
phrases.english: Shimon ben Azzai and Shimon ben Zoma,
and Ḥanan the Egyptian, and Ḥananya ben Ḥakhinai.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second item in the list of code phrases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Judged before the חכמים' refers to these four.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק counts five
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק teaches the list with five names: three named שמעון, plus חנן and חנניה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק taught five: שמעון, שמעון, and שמעון, חנן, and חנניה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the list that adds one more name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra name is the third שמעון, who is שמעון התימני from step 4. That fits, since he was described there as 'judging before them.'

keyTerms.meaning: Teaches, meaning he has this version of the list
Five

phrases.aramaic: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק מַתְנֵי חֲמִשָּׁה:
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak would teach five:
Shimon, Shimon, and Shimon, Ḥanan, and Ḥananya.
phrases.notes: The third שמעון is שמעון התימני, who sat on the ground in יבנה.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק מַתְנֵי חֲמִשָּׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of the list in step 8, adding שמעון התימני.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The list has five names, including שמעון התימני.
steps.whatToRemember: 'Judged before the חכמים' means top students who discussed cases before the judges. רב נחמן בר יצחק adds שמעון התימני to the list.

steps.title: Code names for 'our Rabbis' and 'the judges' of each place
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא continues its list. 'Our Rabbis in בבל' means רב and שמואל, and 'our Rabbis in ארץ ישראל' means רבי אבא. 'The judges' of the גולה, ארץ ישראל, פומבדיתא and נהרדעא each refer to specific חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Our Rabbis in בבל' means רב and שמואל. 'Our Rabbis in ארץ ישראל' means רבי אבא. 'The judges of the גולה' means קרנא. 'The judges of ארץ ישראל' means רבי אמי and רבי אסי. 'The judges of פומבדיתא' means רב פפא בר שמואל. 'The judges of נהרדעא' means רב אדא בר מניומי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps decoding titles you will see around ש״ס. It tells you which real חכמים are meant by phrases like 'our Rabbis' and 'the judges' of a certain place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sometimes a statement is quoted under a title instead of a name. This list tells you exactly who said it. Each line has the same shape: the title, a dash, then the name.

keyTerms.meaning: Our Rabbis (a title of honor)
Judges
The Diaspora, the Jewish community outside ארץ ישראל
פומבדיתא, a major Torah center in בבל
נהרדעא, another major Torah center in בבל

phrases.english: 'Our Rabbis in Babylonia' – Rav and Shmuel.
'Our Rabbis in the Land of Israel' – Rabbi Abba.
'The judges of the Diaspora' – Karna.

phrases.aramaic: דַּיָּינֵי דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל – רַבִּי אַמֵּי וְרַבִּי אַסִּי.
phrases.english: 'The judges of the Land of Israel' – Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi.

phrases.aramaic: דַּיָּינֵי דְּפוּמְבְּדִיתָא – רַב פָּפָּא בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל.
phrases.english: 'The judges of Pumbedita' – Rav Pappa bar Shmuel.

phrases.aramaic: דַּיָּינֵי דִּנְהַרְדְּעָא – רַב אַדָּא בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי.
phrases.english: 'The judges of Neharde'a' – Rav Adda bar Minyumi.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of code phrases begun in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Titles like 'our Rabbis' and 'the judges' of a place each stand for specific named חכמים.

steps.title: Code names for the elders, the sharp ones, and the אמוראים
steps.stepSummary: 'The elders of סורא' are רב הונא and רב חסדא. 'The elders of פומבדיתא' are רב יהודה and רב עינא. 'The sharp ones of פומבדיתא' are עיפה and אבימי. 'The אמוראים of פומבדיתא' are רבה and רב יוסף, and 'the אמוראים of נהרדעא' means רב חמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The elders of סורא' means רב הונא and רב חסדא. 'The elders of פומבדיתא' means רב יהודה and רב עינא. 'The sharp ones of פומבדיתא' means עיפה and אבימי, the sons of רחבה. 'The אמוראים of פומבדיתא' means רבה and רב יוסף. 'The אמוראים of נהרדעא' means רב חמא.
steps.whatsHappening: The list goes on with more titles: elders, sharp-minded scholars, and אמוראים of certain cities. Each title is matched to the real people it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is being argued yet. The גמרא is simply adding more entries to the list. Note that one city, פומבדיתא, has several different groups, each with its own title.

keyTerms.meaning: Elders
סורא, a major yeshiva city in בבל
The sharp ones, the quick-minded scholars
אמוראים, the חכמים of the גמרא period

phrases.aramaic: סָבֵי דְּסוּרָא – רַב הוּנָא וְרַב חִסְדָּא.
phrases.english: 'The elders of Sura' – Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda.

phrases.aramaic: סָבֵי דְּפוּמְבְּדִיתָא – רַב יְהוּדָה וְרַב עֵינָא.
phrases.english: 'The elders of Pumbedita' – Rav Yehuda and Rav Eina.

phrases.aramaic: חֲרִיפֵי דְּפוּמְבְּדִיתָא – עֵיפָה וַאֲבִימִי בְּנֵי רַחֲבָה.
phrases.english: 'The sharp ones of Pumbedita' – Eifa and Avimi, the sons of Raḥava.
'The amora'im of Pumbedita' – Rabba and Rav Yosef.
'The amora'im of Neharde'a' – Rav Ḥama.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבֵי דְּסוּרָא – רַב הוּנָא וְרַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more entries to the same list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Titles of elders, sharp scholars and אמוראים of each city refer to specific חכמים.

steps.title: Who is meant by 'נהרבלאי מתנו' and 'they say in the school of רב'
steps.stepSummary: 'The people of נהרבל taught' means רמי בר ברבי. 'They say in the school of רב' is first identified as רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The people of נהרבל taught' means רמי בר ברבי. 'They say in the school of רב' means רב הונא.
steps.whatsHappening: The list now turns to phrases that introduce a teaching. One of these answers, רב הונא, is about to be challenged, so this step is setting up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These phrases describe how a teaching was passed on: 'taught,' 'they say.' The identification of 'אמרי בי רב' as רב הונא will be tested right away in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: They say in the school (yeshiva) of רב

phrases.english: 'The people of Neharbela taught' – Rami bar Berabi.
'They say in the school of Rav' – Rav Huna.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list and sets up a challenge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'נהרבלאי מתנו' is רמי בר ברבי. 'אמרי בי רב' is first said to be רב הונא.

steps.title: But רב הונא himself quotes 'they say in the school of רב'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects. רב הונא himself sometimes says 'אמרי בי רב,' so the phrase cannot be a code name for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רב הונא himself says, 'They say in the school of רב'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that 'אמרי בי רב' means רב הונא. We find רב הונא himself using that phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רב הונא opens a teaching with 'they say in the school of רב,' he is quoting someone else. So the phrase must point to a different person.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? (opens a challenge from a known statement)

phrases.english: But Rav Huna himself says: 'They say in the school of Rav'!
phrases.notes: If רב הונא uses this phrase, he is quoting someone else, so it can't be his own code name.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמְרִי בֵּי רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the identification made in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'אמרי בי רב' refers to רב הונא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person does not quote himself with a phrase that points to others. Since רב הונא uses the phrase, it must refer to someone else.

steps.title: Correction: it means רב המנונא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects itself. 'אמרי בי רב' refers to רב המנונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means רב המנונא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the first answer and gives a new name: רב המנונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge proved that רב הונא cannot be the meaning. The word 'אלא' (rather) signals that the earlier answer is replaced, not just explained.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (replaces the earlier answer)

phrases.english: Rather, it is Rav Hamnuna.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13 by changing the name.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'אמרי בי רב' was thought to mean רב הונא.

steps.title: Code names for phrases from ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: 'They say in the West' means רבי ירמיה. 'They sent from there' is first said to mean רבי יוסי בר חנינא. 'They laughed at it in the West' is first said to mean רבי אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They say in the West' means רבי ירמיה. 'They sent from there' means רבי יוסי בר חנינא. 'They laughed at it in the West' means רבי אלעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now decodes phrases that come from ארץ ישראל. Two of these identifications will soon be challenged, so this step is setting up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The West' and 'there' both mean ארץ ישראל, as seen from בבל. 'Laughed at it' means a חכם there rejected a teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: The West, meaning ארץ ישראל
They sent from there (a message from ארץ ישראל)
They laughed at it, meaning they rejected it

phrases.english: 'They say in the West' – Rabbi Yirmeya.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלַחוּ מִתָּם – רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא.
phrases.english: 'They sent from there' – Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina.
'They laughed at it in the West' – Rabbi Elazar.
phrases.notes: Laughing here means they didn't accept the idea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the list after the correction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first identifications: 'אמרי במערבא' is רבי ירמיה, 'שלחו מתם' is רבי יוסי בר חנינא, and 'מחכו עלה במערבא' is רבי אלעזר.

steps.title: But a message 'sent from there' quotes רבי יוסי בר חנינא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects. One message sent from ארץ ישראל says 'according to the words of רבי יוסי בר חנינא,' so he can't be the sender.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we find: 'They sent from there: according to the words of רבי יוסי בר חנינא'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that 'שלחו מתם' means רבי יוסי בר חנינא. A message sent from there actually quotes him by name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the senders quote רבי יוסי בר חנינא, then the senders are someone else. It is the same kind of challenge as the one against רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the words of

phrases.english: But they sent from there:
'According to the words of Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina'!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא שְׁלַחוּ מִתָּם לְדִבְרֵי רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks one identification from step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'שלחו מתם' refers to רבי יוסי בר חנינא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A message that quotes רבי יוסי בר חנינא by name must come from someone else.

steps.title: Swap the two names
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reverses the two identifications. 'שלחו מתם' is רבי אלעזר, and 'מחכו עלה במערבא' is רבי יוסי בר חנינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, reverse it. 'They sent from there' means רבי אלעזר. 'They laughed at it in the West' means רבי יוסי בר חנינא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by switching the two names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now 'שלחו מתם' points to רבי אלעזר, so a message that quotes רבי יוסי בר חנינא is no longer a problem. The two names trade places, and nobody new is added.

keyTerms.meaning: Reverse it, switch the two

steps.whatToRemember: Final list for ארץ ישראל: 'אמרי במערבא' is רבי ירמיה, 'שלחו מתם' is רבי אלעזר, and 'מחכו עלה במערבא' is רבי יוסי בר חנינא. Also, 'אמרי בי רב' is רב המנונא.

phrases.english: Rather, reverse it:
'They sent from there' – Rabbi Elazar;

phrases.aramaic: מַחֲכוּ עֲלַהּ בְּמַעְרְבָא – רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא.
phrases.english: 'They laughed at it in the West' – Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by switching the two names.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'שלחו מתם' was רבי יוסי בר חנינא and 'מחכו עלה' was רבי אלעזר.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'שלחו מתם' is רבי אלעזר and 'מחכו עלה' is רבי יוסי בר חנינא.

steps.title: Why does a city need 120 men?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the משנה, which says a city needs 120 men to have a סנהדרין קטנה. It asks what all 120 people are for.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'How many must be in a city for it to be fit for a סנהדרין? 120, and so on.' What are these 120 needed for?
steps.whatsHappening: The list is over. The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule of 120 men and asks why that exact number is needed. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סנהדרין קטנה has only 23 judges, so 120 seems like a lot. The גמרא wants to know which jobs or roles add up to 120.

keyTerms.meaning: A court that rules on capital cases
Fit, eligible
What is their purpose? What are they for?

phrases.english: And how many must be in the city
for it to be fit for a Sanhedrin?
One hundred and twenty, etc.
One hundred and twenty: what are they for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the list of names and starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the 120 men required by the משנה are needed for.

steps.title: Starting the count: 23 judges, three rows, and ten בטלנין
steps.stepSummary: The 23 judges, plus three rows of 23 students, make 92. Ten בטלנין of the בית הכנסת bring the total to 102.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are 23 for the סנהדרין קטנה itself. There are three rows of 23 students in front of them, which makes 92. There are ten בטלנין of the בית הכנסת, which makes 102.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts adding up the people a city needs: the judges, the rows of students sitting before them, and ten people always free for the בית הכנסת. So far the total is 102, not yet 120.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 23 judges plus 3 × 23 students equals 92, and 10 בטלנין make 102. The count is not finished yet; the גמרא still has 18 more people to account for.

keyTerms.meaning: The small סנהדרין of 23 judges
Rows (of students sitting before the court)
People free from work who are always available for the בית הכנסת

steps.confusionAlert: Here בטלנין is not an insult meaning 'lazy people.' It means people who are free from other work so they can always be at the בית הכנסת for the community's needs.

phrases.english: Twenty-three corresponding to the lesser Sanhedrin,
and three rows of twenty-three –
that is ninety-two,
and ten idlers of the synagogue –
that is one hundred and two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: So far: 23 judges, plus 69 students in three rows, plus 10 בטלנין, for a total of 102. The rest of the count follows.

steps.title: Adding court staff and witnesses brings the count to 114
steps.stepSummary: The count goes on from 102. It adds two scribes, two court attendants, two litigants, two witnesses, two witnesses who could make them זוממין, and two more who could make those זוממין. The total is now 114.
steps.simpleTranslation: And two scribes, two court attendants, two litigants, two witnesses, two witnesses who make them זוממין, and two who make those זוממין. That makes 114.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps adding up the people a סנהדרין needs, continuing from the 102 counted in the last step. It now reaches 114.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A court cannot work with only judges and students. It needs staff and people to judge, and it needs witnesses. It also needs the people who could prove those witnesses false, and the people who could prove that second pair false. These twelve people are added to the earlier 102.

keyTerms.meaning: Scribes who write down the court's proceedings
Court attendants or bailiffs
The two sides in a court case (litigants)
False witnesses, shown to be lying by other witnesses who say 'you were with us somewhere else'
Witnesses who prove that the second pair of witnesses were themselves lying

phrases.english: And two scribes, and two court attendants,
and two litigants, and two witnesses,
and two who make them conspiring witnesses,
phrases.notes: These two come and say the first witnesses were with them somewhere else at the time, so the first pair is lying.

phrases.english: and two who make those witnesses conspiring witnesses,
that makes one hundred and fourteen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the answer from step 19, going from 102 up to 114.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who makes up the 120 people the משנה requires?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Two scribes, two attendants, two litigants, and three pairs of witnesses bring the total to 114.

steps.title: A ברייתא listing ten things every city must have
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: a תלמיד חכם may not live in a city without ten things. The list starts with a court that can punish and a charity fund collected by two and handed out by three. It goes on with a בית הכנסת, a bathhouse, and a public bathroom. It ends with a doctor, a bloodletter, a scribe, a שוחט, and a teacher of children. These extra required people fill in the count up to 120.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it was taught: a תלמיד חכם may not live in any city that does not have these ten things. They are a court that can whip and punish, a charity fund collected by two and handed out by three, a בית הכנסת, a bathhouse, a bathroom, a doctor, a bloodletter, a scribe, a שוחט, and a teacher of young children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists what every proper city must have. It uses this list to supply the last few people needed to reach 120.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The count so far was 114, but the משנה said 120. Some items on this list need people who live in the city, like the charity workers, the doctor, the bloodletter, the שוחט and the teacher. Adding them fills the gap up to 120, although the גמרא does not spell out the exact math.

keyTerms.meaning: A Torah scholar
Whipping and punishing: a court with real power to enforce the law
The community charity fund
A bloodletter (someone who lets blood for healing)
A scribe who writes documents
A teacher of young children

phrases.english: And it was taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל עִיר שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ עֲשָׂרָה דְּבָרִים הַלָּלוּ
phrases.english: Any city that does not have these ten things

phrases.aramaic: אֵין תַּלְמִיד חָכָם רַשַּׁאי לָדוּר בְּתוֹכָהּ:
phrases.english: a Torah scholar is not allowed to live in it:
a court that whips and punishes,
and a charity fund that is collected by two people
and handed out by three,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת, וּבֵית הַמֶּרְחָץ, וּבֵית הַכִּסֵּא,
phrases.english: and a synagogue, and a bathhouse, and a bathroom,
a doctor, and a bloodletter, and a scribe,
and a slaughterer, and a teacher of young children.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנְיָא: כׇּל עִיר שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ עֲשָׂרָה דְּבָרִים הַלָּלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies a ברייתא whose required people complete the count from 114 to 120.
steps.raayaObject: That a city large enough for a סנהדרין must also contain more residents beyond the 114 already counted
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the ten things a city needs for a תלמיד חכם to live there
steps.whatToRemember: The 120 people of the משנה come from two groups: the court with its students, staff and witnesses (114), plus the basic workers every proper city needs.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rest of the 120 are the residents every proper city needs according to the ברייתא, such as the charity distributors, the doctor, the bloodletter, the scribe, the שוחט and the teacher.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא adds different kinds of fruit
steps.stepSummary: In the name of רבי עקיבא they said that a city must also have different kinds of fruit. The reason is that fruit brightens the eyes.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said in the name of רבי עקיבא: also different kinds of fruit, because different kinds of fruit brighten the eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: Still inside the ברייתא, רבי עקיבא adds one more thing a city needs: a variety of fruit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This addition is not about people, so it does not change the count of 120. It shows that the list is about a healthy, livable city. Fruit is included because it is good for a person's health and eyesight.

keyTerms.meaning: They said in the name of רבי עקיבא
Different kinds of fruit
Brighten the eyes (good for health and eyesight)

phrases.english: They said in the name of Rabbi Akiva:
also different kinds of fruit,

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמִּינֵי פֵירָא מְאִירִין אֶת הָעֵינַיִם.
phrases.english: because different kinds of fruit brighten the eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: An addition to the list in the ברייתא from step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי עקיבא, a proper city must also have a variety of fruit, because fruit brightens the eyes.

steps.title: Turning to רבי נחמיה's opinion in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the start of רבי נחמיה's opinion from the משנה. It then begins a ברייתא in the name of רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי נחמיה says, and so on. It was taught: רבי says:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next opinion in the משנה, that of רבי נחמיה. This line is setting up the next move: a ברייתא from רבי, whose words continue right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The discussion of the 120 is finished, so the גמרא turns to רבי נחמיה, who requires a different number of people in the משנה. Quoting a ברייתא of רבי here gets ready to explain or add to that opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And so on': the rest of the quote is in the משנה

phrases.english: Rabbi Nehemya says, and so on.
phrases.notes: In the משנה, רבי נחמיה says the city needs 230 men.

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi says:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the count of 120 behind and turns to the next opinion in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduces a ברייתא from רבי about רבי נחמיה's opinion; the content follows next.
